classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied sine substitution, rewrite the remaining cosine square with a standard identity, transform limits and integrate powers.

content.prompt: Evaluate each definite integral using $u=\sin x$.

answer.worked:
Let $u=\sin x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{du}{dx}&=\cos x\\dx&=\frac{du}{\cos x}\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$, $u=0$; when $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$, $u=\frac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\pi/6}\frac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}\,dx&=\int_0^{1/2}\frac{1}{1+u}\,du\\&=\left[\ln|1+u|\right]_0^{1/2}\\&=\ln\left(\frac32\right)-\ln1\\&=\ln\left(\frac32\right)\end{aligned}$$

Let $u=\sin x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{du}{dx}&=\cos x\\dx&=\frac{du}{\cos x}\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$, $u=0$; when $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $u=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos x}{1+\sin^2x}\,dx&=\int_0^1\frac{1}{1+u^2}\,du\\&=\left[\tan^{-1}u\right]_0^1\\&=\frac\pi4-0\\&=\frac\pi4\end{aligned}$$

Let $u=\sin x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{du}{dx}&=\cos x\\dx&=\frac{du}{\cos x}\\\cos^2x&=1-u^2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$, $u=0$; when $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $u=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^3x\,dx&=\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2x\cos x\,dx\\&=\int_0^1(1-u^2)\,du\\&=\left[u-\frac{u^3}{3}\right]_0^1\\&=1-\frac13\\&=\frac23\end{aligned}$$

Let $u=\sin x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{du}{dx}&=\cos x\\dx&=\frac{du}{\cos x}\\\cos^2x&=1-u^2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$, $u=\frac{1}{2}$; when $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $u=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^3x}{\sin^4x}\,dx&=\int_{1/2}^1\frac{1-u^2}{u^4}\,du\\&=\int_{1/2}^1(u^{-4}-u^{-2})\,du\\&=\left[-\frac{1}{3u^3}+\frac1u\right]_{1/2}^1\\&=\left(-\frac13+1\right)-\left(-\frac83+2\right)\\&=\frac43\end{aligned}$$
